title: The Fossil Dig
sum: Nora spends a week digging at a fossil quarry, hoping for a whole trilobite, and on the last day her little brother finds one that only she can recognize.

cast.d: a nine-year-old girl who wants to find a whole trilobite
cast.look: a nine-year-old girl with a long brown braid, a straw sun hat, dusty knees and a green notebook

cast.d: Nora's six-year-old brother, who collects fossil 'buttons'
cast.look: a six-year-old boy with messy blond hair, a red T-shirt and a big orange bucket

cast.d: Nora and Leo's mom, a carpenter who always carries a tape measure
cast.look: a woman with a dark ponytail, work boots and a yellow tape measure on her belt

cast.d: the kids' grandpa, the Chief Checker in a camp chair
cast.look: an older man with a white beard, a floppy fishing hat and a magnifying glass as big as a pancake

cast.d: the busy park ranger at Stony Hollow Fossil Park
cast.look: a woman with short curly black hair, a green ranger hat and a coffee cup

p: The gravel road ended at a wooden sign: STONY HOLLOW FOSSIL PARK. Behind it stood a tall wall of gray rock, striped like a layer cake. Nora had a new green notebook and a pencil behind her ear. Her little brother Leo had a bucket almost as big as he was.

A ranger in a green hat met the family at the gate. Her name tag said RANGER DEE, and she talked fast, like someone with forty families to see. “Long ago, this whole place was the bottom of a warm sea,” she said. “Everything you find here lived in the water.” Then she handed Nora a small card that said FOSSIL CLUES.
RIBS: a sea shell. BUTTONS: a piece of a sea lily. HORN: a horn coral. THREE LOBES: a trilobite. Next to the last clue was a drawing of something like a big, flat pill bug.
“I want one of these,” Nora said. “A whole one, this week.” Ranger Dee raised her eyebrows. “Most people only find a piece, if they're lucky.”

Nora wrote WHOLE TRILOBITE at the top of her first page and drew an empty box next to it. Then Mom pulled out her tape and marked a dig patch 4 meters long and 3 meters wide. Nora pushed in a stick at every meter while Leo helped tie the string. Soon the patch looked like a giant waffle, with every square 1 meter on each side.

Nora took the row beside the rock wall, and Leo took the row beside the snack bag. Grandpa Walt settled into his camp chair at the edge, holding a magnifying glass as big as a pancake. “I'm the Chief Checker,” he said. “My knees are staying here.”
Nora picked up a flat gray rock and hit the top with her hammer. It broke into crumbs. She tried again and got more crumbs, plus a puff of dust up her nose.
Leo lugged bucket after bucket over to Grandpa, who checked each rock under the glass. “Rock,” he said. “Another rock. A very nice rock.”
Ranger Dee stopped beside Nora's row. “You're knocking on the front door,” she said. “Try the side.” She pushed a flat screwdriver into the edge of a rock and tapped it twice.

The rock split open like a book. “Shale is mud that got pressed flat, layer on layer,” said Ranger Dee. “It likes to split along the layers.” She left the screwdriver with Nora and hurried off. Nora's next rock opened on the second tap, smooth and gray and empty inside.
After twenty minutes, Nora's knees hurt, and Leo was digging in her row. “Hey, that's my row!” she said. “The rocks don't know that,” said Leo, but he took one giant step back anyway.

Nora slid the screwdriver into one more rock and gave it two taps. Inside was a little fan shape, no bigger than her thumbnail, with thin lines across it like ribs. She jumped up so fast that her sun hat fell off. “Grandpa! RIBS!”
Grandpa bent over it with the big glass. “That's a sea shell, all right.” “About 380 million years old,” Ranger Dee called on her way past.
Leo's eyes went wide. “Older than Grandpa?” “A little,” said Grandpa.

By lunch, Grandpa had checked 30 of Leo's rocks. One of them held a real fossil: a tiny round button with a hole in the middle. Under the empty box, Nora wrote: Monday — 1 shell, 1 button, 0 bugs. Then she laid her shell in an egg carton, all by itself in the first cup.

art.s: A girl kneeling in a string grid on a gray quarry floor holds up a split rock with a tiny ribbed shell, while her little brother runs by with a big bucket and a grandpa watches from a camp chair with a huge magnifying glass.

q.q: Why did Ranger Dee tap the edge of the rock instead of the top?
c: Shale splits apart along its layers
The top of a rock is too hard
Fossils only hide near the edges
Tapping the top makes too much noise
q.e: Shale is mud pressed flat, layer on layer. A tap on the edge opens it like a book.

q.q: Draw the FOSSIL CLUES card. Next to each clue word, draw the fossil it means.
look: the four clue words: RIBS, BUTTONS, HORN, THREE LOBES
a shell, a sea lily button, a horn coral and a trilobite
each fossil next to its own clue word
q.e: RIBS for the shell, BUTTONS for the sea lily, HORN for the coral, THREE LOBES for the trilobite. Each word tells you what shape to look for!

q.q: The dig patch was 4 meters long and 3 meters wide. Each square was 1 meter on each side. How many squares were there?
q.e: Three rows of 4 squares make 12 squares.

p: On Tuesday, Leo only wanted buttons. He crawled along his row with his nose almost on the ground, like a puppy hunting for crumbs. Once he knew what to look for, the little round buttons seemed to be everywhere. By ten o'clock, he had 9 of them rattling in a yogurt cup.
Leo held up the cup and gave it a shake. “Snake bones,” he told Nora. “I touched a snake at the zoo, and its back felt just like these!”
Nora didn't even look up. “They're from a sea lily. It says so right on the card.” “A lily is a flower,” said Leo, “and flowers don't have bones.”

They went back and forth like that until Grandpa put down his magnifying glass. “Sounds like a job for the visitor center,” he said. “Also, they have a bathroom.” Leo grabbed his yogurt cup and marched off first.

The visitor center was a small wooden building with a fan humming in the window. In a glass case lay a slab of rock as long as a bicycle. Pressed into it was a thin stem made of buttons, stacked up like coins.
At the top of the stem was a cup with feathery arms, spread out like the petals of a flower. “See?” said Leo. “It IS a flower.”

Ranger Dee sat behind the desk with a cup of coffee and a ringing telephone. “It looks like one,” she said, “but it was an animal. Those arms caught tiny bits of food as the water drifted by.” Leo stared at the feathery arms for a long time. Then he waved his own arms in the air, catching invisible snacks.

Nora pressed her nose to the glass. “Why is the stem in so many pieces?” Ranger Dee covered the telephone with her hand. “A stem made of little pieces can bend,” she said. “When the water pushed, the sea lily swayed instead of snapping.”

Back at the picnic table, Grandpa had a box of cereal rings and an idea. He threaded 20 rings onto a spare shoelace and tied a knot at the bottom. When Leo held it by the top and wiggled it, the cereal stem swayed like a tiny sea lily.

Nora tried the same wiggle with a pencil, but the pencil stayed stiff. When she pushed harder, it made a small cracking sound. “Don't snap it,” said Mom. “So that's why it's in pieces,” said Nora. Leo didn't answer, because he was busy eating his sea lily from the top down.

After lunch, Leo found his best button yet. It was not one button but 8 buttons still stuck together, like a short roll of coins. “How long is it?” he asked. Mom measured a single button first: 4 millimeters thick.
Nora started working it out in the dirt with a stick: 8 × 4… Leo couldn't wait, so he held the piece against Mom's tape instead. Same number!
“Some sea lilies grew taller than Grandpa,” said Mom. “I read it on the sign.” Grandpa sat up a little straighter in his camp chair.

Before they went home, Nora wrote a new label for Leo's yogurt cup: SEA LILY BUTTONS. Leo took the pencil. Nora spelled it out, and letter by letter he added one more word underneath: ANIMAL. Then he leaned close to the cup and whispered, “Sorry I called you snakes.”

art.s: In a small wooden visitor center, a boy holding a yogurt cup and his older sister press their noses to a glass case that holds a fossil sea lily with a long stem of stacked buttons and feathery arms.

q.q: Leo's piece was 8 buttons stuck together. Each button was 4 millimeters thick. How long was the piece?
c: 12 mm
24 mm
32 mm
48 mm
q.e: 8 × 4 = 32. The piece was 32 mm long, about as long as a paper clip.

q.q: Why was the sea lily's stem made of so many little pieces?
q.a: So it could bend and sway when the water pushed, instead of snapping.
q.e: Little pieces can bend, like cereal rings on a shoelace. A stiff pencil just cracks.

q.q: Draw Leo and Nora arguing about the buttons. In each speech bubble, write what they think and why.
look: Leo holding up his yogurt cup of buttons
Leo's bubble: snake bones, because a snake's back felt like these
Nora's bubble: sea lily, because the card says so
q.e: Leo had a reason, and Nora had a reason. The glass case at the visitor center settled it.

p: On Wednesday morning, a big yellow digger rumbled across the far end of the quarry. It scraped along the bottom of the rock wall and dumped a fresh pile of broken stone. Beep, beep, beep went the digger as it backed away. Ranger Dee climbed down from the driver's seat and pulled off her work gloves.
“New pile, straight from the bug bed,” she said. Leo's mouth fell open. “Bugs have beds?”
He found the flattest rock on the ground and lay down on it to try it out. “Way too lumpy,” he said. Grandpa laughed until his fishing hat slid over one eye. “No wonder the bugs moved out.”

“Not that kind of bed,” said Ranger Dee. “In a quarry, a bed is a layer of rock.” She pointed to a thin brown stripe low on the wall. “That's the bug bed, where we find most of our trilobites.” Then her radio crackled, and she hurried off again.

Rule number one at Stony Hollow was no climbing on the wall, so Mom measured from the ground. The brown bug bed was easy, only 8 centimeters thick. For the gray shale above it, she had to push the stiff tape up over her head. “240 centimeters,” she said. “Taller than Grandpa with his hat on.”

Leo squinted up at the stripes. “How many bug beds would it take to make one gray one?” Nora opened her notebook and wrote 240 ÷ 8. She had only just started when Leo asked something else. “Which one is older?”
Grandpa answered with a question of his own. “What's at the bottom of our laundry basket at home?” “Socks from last week,” said Nora. Mom groaned, because it was true.
Grandpa pointed at the wall. “Mud piled up on the old sea floor the same way, one layer at a time. The bottom layers went in first, so they're the oldest.”
Nora looked from the bottom of the wall to the top. Dark shale, then the brown bug bed, then all that gray. So the trilobites were down there first, long before the gray mud buried them.

They carried their buckets over to the new pile. The brown rocks were much harder than the gray shale. When Nora tapped one, it rang like a dinner plate instead of going thud. She had to tap so hard to open it that her whole hand buzzed.

Mom found a horn coral, shaped like a little ice cream cone with lines down the side. Leo climbed to the top of the pile and sang to the rocks. “Wake up, bugs! It's breakfast time!” A boy from the next patch laughed so hard that he dropped his brush.

Nora opened one more brown rock. Inside was a curved piece shaped like a half-moon, about as wide as a nickel. Three ridges ran down it, one in the middle and one on each side. Three lobes! Nora held her breath and carried it to Grandpa with both hands.

Grandpa looked through the glass for a long time. “Trilobite,” he said at last. “The tail end.” Nora looked at the empty box in her notebook, but she didn't check it. Instead, she wrote: Wednesday — 1 bug (back half).

“Half a bug is still more bug than yesterday,” said Grandpa. Nora laughed and laid the tail in the egg carton, right next to her very first shell. Leo peered into the carton. “Where's the front half?”

art.s: At the foot of a striped quarry wall, a mom holds a tape measure up to a thin brown rock layer while a small boy lies flat on a rock and a yellow digger backs away from a fresh pile of stone.

q.q: The gray shale was 240 cm thick. The bug bed was 8 cm thick. How many bug beds would stack up as tall as the gray shale?
Ranger Dee talked about the bug bed. What does bed mean in a quarry?
q.e: A bed can be where you sleep, or a layer of rock. Leo found out the rock kind is too lumpy!

q.q: Draw the quarry wall with its layers, from bottom to top. Put a star on the oldest layer.
look: layers stacked on top of each other
the thin brown bug bed near the bottom
a star on the bottom layer
q.e: The bottom layer went down first, so it's the oldest, like last week's socks at the bottom of the basket.

p: It rained all night. On Thursday morning, the quarry floor was dark and shiny and smelled like a wet sidewalk. Leo stomped in every puddle in their squares while Nora stared at her notebook. Only two days were left, and the box next to WHOLE TRILOBITE was still empty.
By ten o'clock, Nora had found a head piece with one bumpy eye, like the top of a raspberry. Leo found a thin strip from the middle of a bug, with little ridges across it like a zipper. Pieces again.
Leo had borrowed Mom's hammer, and he liked it a lot, maybe too much. Whack, whack! Chips flew off his rocks like popcorn from a pot with no lid.
“Stop smashing them!” Nora yelled across the squares. “You're breaking all the bugs!” Leo's lower lip began to wobble.
“I didn't break it,” he said. “It was already like that inside.” Nora didn't believe him, so she took the hammer out of his hand and hid it behind her back.
Ranger Dee came by with her coffee and bent over the pieces. “He's right, you know,” she said. “These came apart a very long time ago, way before anybody had a hammer.”
She tapped the head piece with one finger. “A trilobite had a hard shell, like a crab. To grow bigger, it wriggled out and left the old shell lying on the sea floor. Empty shells fall apart easily.”
“So one bug could leave lots of shells?” asked Leo. “Lots,” said Ranger Dee. “Most of the pieces in this quarry are old shells. Nobody was home.”
As Ranger Dee walked on to the next family, Nora's face went hot. She pulled the hammer from behind her back and held it out to Leo, handle first. “Sorry, Leo. You didn't break them.”
Leo took the hammer back and pointed at a little heap of crumbs. “I did break that one,” he said. “But it was just a rock.”

After that, they split the job. Leo took the hammer and the gray rocks, which were mostly empty anyway. Nora took the screwdriver and the brown ones, tapping along the edges the way Ranger Dee had shown her.

At lunch, Nora made a table of everything the family had found so far. It had four rows: 8 shells with ribs, 12 buttons, 4 horn corals and 3 bug pieces. Then she turned it into a bar graph on squared paper, one square for each fossil.

Leo slid his finger from the top of the button bar down, down, down to the bug bar. “The bug bar is a baby,” he said. Grandpa tapped the tallest bar with his magnifying glass. “Buttons are easy. Bugs are hard.”

“Then how does anybody find a whole one?” Nora asked as Ranger Dee passed their table. “You need one that got buried in mud all at once,” said Ranger Dee, “before it came apart. Sometimes they rolled up first, like pill bugs.”

Leo dropped his sandwich and dove under the picnic table. He came back with a tiny gray ball on his flat palm. “Look, Nora,” he said. “A whole one.” The ball unrolled, waved its fourteen little legs and walked right off his thumb.

art.s: At a picnic table beside a wet gray quarry, a small boy holds out a rolled-up pill bug on his palm while his sister laughs over a notebook with a bar graph and three trilobite pieces.

q.q: Why did Nora say sorry to Leo?
q.a: She yelled that he was breaking the bugs, but the pieces were old shells that were already broken long ago.
q.e: Leo didn't break them. The trilobites had left those old shells behind a very long time ago.

q.q: Why did the family find so many trilobite pieces?
c: Trilobites left old shells behind as they grew
The rain broke the trilobites into bits
Leo smashed them all with the hammer
The digger crushed them in the pile
q.e: To grow bigger, a trilobite wriggled out of its old shell, like a crab. Old shells fall apart easily.

q.q: Draw Nora's bar graph: 8 shells, 12 buttons, 4 horn corals and 3 bug pieces. How many more buttons than bug pieces did they find?
look: four bars, each with a label
the button bar 12 squares tall and the bug bar 3 squares tall
q.e: 12 − 3 = 9. Nine more buttons than bugs! No wonder a trilobite is such a big find.

p: Friday was the last day, and everything took too long. The tent had to come down and the car had to be packed. Leo lost a shoe. It turned up in the cooler, under the hot dogs.
“That car looks like a suitcase that ate too much,” said Grandpa. By the time they reached their squares, Mom's watch said 2:15. The park closed at 3:00.

Nora went straight to the bug bed pile, because this time she knew what to do. Brown rock, screwdriver in the edge, tap, tap, look for three lobes. One after another, the brown rocks rang like dinner plates. Every one was empty.
Nora's fingers turned gray with dust, and a breeze kept blowing grit into her eyes. At 2:40, Mom called out, “Twenty minutes!” Nora's hands started to shake a little on the screwdriver.
Leo waddled over with his yogurt cup in one hand and a lumpy gray pebble in the other. “Biggest button ever,” he said, holding it up to her nose. “It doesn't even have a hole.”

He was about to drop it into the cup when Nora saw two tiny bumps on one side. They looked like the tops of two raspberries, just like the eye on Thursday's head piece. Eyes! She took the pebble and turned it over. Across its back ran three lobes, a ridge in the middle and one on each side.

“Grandpa,” Nora said, but it came out as a squeak. Grandpa held the glass so close that it almost touched the stone, then let out a long, low whistle. “Trilobite,” he said. “A whole one, rolled up tight.” Mom held up her tape: 3 centimeters across, about the size of a big grape.

Ranger Dee set down her coffee for the first time all week. “Look at that,” she said. “Something scared it, so it curled up. Hard shell on the outside, soft legs and belly tucked in. Then mud covered it before it could unroll.”
Leo stood very still. “I found it,” he said. Nora looked at the trilobite in her palm, then at her little brother. Her throat felt tight. All week she had wanted to find one herself.
“You found it,” she said. “But I almost put it with the buttons,” said Leo. “You knew what it was.”

Ranger Dee took a photo of it for the Find of the Week board. Then Nora wrote a label for the egg carton in her best letters. Her first try just said TRILOBITE, which felt too short for something so old. Her second try said ROLLED-UP TRILOBITE, ABOUT 380 MILLION YEARS OLD. At the bottom, she added: Found by Leo, figured out by Nora.

At 3:00, Ranger Dee turned the sign on the gate to CLOSED. Nora opened her notebook and put a big check in the box next to WHOLE TRILOBITE. She pressed so hard that the pencil poked right through the page.
Leo shook his yogurt cup like a rattle. “Next year,” he said, “a whole sea lily.” Grandpa looked over at the stuffed car. “Then we'll need a bigger one.”

art.s: A girl holds a tiny rolled-up trilobite fossil on her open palm while her little brother with a yogurt cup, a grandpa with a big magnifying glass and a ranger with a coffee cup lean in close.

q.q: What is this chapter mostly about?
c: How Nora and Leo found a whole trilobite
How Leo lost his shoe in the cooler
How the family packed up the tent
How the park closed at three o'clock
q.e: Lots of things happened, but the big one was the whole trilobite: found by Leo, figured out by Nora.

q.q: They started digging at 2:15. The park closed at 3:00. How many minutes did they have to dig?
q.e: From 2:15 to 3:00 is 45 minutes. That's three quarters of an hour.

q.q: Draw the trilobite rolled up like a pill bug. Show which part stayed on the outside.
look: a bug curled into a ball
the hard shell on the outside
q.e: Rolled up tight, the hard shell kept its soft legs and belly safe inside.

fin.q: All week, the family found shells, sea lilies, corals and trilobites. What was the quarry long, long ago?
fin.a: The bottom of a warm sea.
fin.e: Every fossil they found was a sea animal. Long ago, the quarry was a sea floor.

fin.q: How did Nora change from Monday to Friday?
c: She learned to read the rocks and their clues
She gave up on finding a trilobite
She started digging far away from Leo
She decided a hammer works best on shale
fin.e: On Monday she got crumbs. By Friday she knew the edges, the layers and the clue words.
